newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Government-backed strike brings Venezuela to a halt.
newsitem.headline: Government-backed strike brings Venezuela to a halt.

text.p: Venezuela virtually ground to a halt on Wednesday as unions staged their first general strike in eight years, a 12-hour stoppage that the government said was justified.

The Venezuelan Workers Confederation (CTV), the country's largest union which organised the walkout to demand wage rises from private sector companies, said initial reports suggested the strike was a success and participation was massive.
"Up to 80 percent of the workforce has joined the strike", CTV President Federico Ramirez Leon told reporters.
Government offices were shut and public transport was almost non-existent in Venezuela's main cities, forcing employees to stay home, radio reports said.
Telephone and electric services were not affected, most banks were opened and airport officials said domestic and international flights were operating normally, with one or two exceptions.
State oil giant Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), which controls the largest oil reserves outside the Middle East, said it maintained normal operations thanks to a contingency plan.
Caracas streets were quieter than usual with armed police and National Guardsmen stationed at certain key installations. There were no reports of incidents.

The stoppage -- the fifth general strike in Venezuela since the country's return to democracy in 1958 -- won the unusual backing of the government of President Rafael Caldera and broad support from across the political spectrum.
Interior Minister Guillermo Andueza said "union leaders are showing a great capacity to fight within the currents of Venezuelan democracy."
Outspoken Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff, who fought a communist guerrilla against the government in the 1960s, reiterated on Wednesday that the strike was "justified".
"The unionized sector must fight for its rights ... this is an alarm bell for the business sector," he told reporters.
Union and government officials have lambasted business leaders for failing to raise salaries as agreed in March in a ground-breaking deal to reform the complex social security system.
But some business leaders ridiculed the government's "lack of seriousness" for endorsing the strike, which was also called to protest last week's 27 percent hike in gasoline prices.

Francisco Natera, head of business chamber Fedecamaras, labeled it "a smokescreen aimed at covering up the government's inability to tackle inflation, fiscal laxity and the constant deterioration of real salaries."
With Venezuela still groggy after three years of recession, runaway inflation and delayed salary rises have cut real wages to one-third of their 1960s level, official figures show.

Business chamber leaders say that 90 percent of their members have increased pay in accordance with the March deal. A commission made up of government, business and union representatives was set up last week to investigate whether these wage hikes have been awarded.
